The requested integer is 499999999972.

First I determine the expected value exactly. For any word of distinct letters, take two letters a<b and consider the contiguous interval in the original word whose endpoints are a and b. The following observation follows from the recursive definition of F:

If the maximum of this interval is b, then a precedes b in F(w). If the interval contains a letter greater than b, then the relative order of a and b in F(w) is their original relative order.

Here is a justification that also handles letters outside the interval. At any step of the recursion, if the maximum of the current word lies outside the interval between the two letters, both letters belong to the same recursive subword. We can therefore descend into that subword. Eventually the maximum is in the interval. If it is b, the definition puts b after every letter of its current subword, including a. Otherwise the maximum lies strictly between the two endpoints and exceeds b. The two letters then lie in the two different recursive subwords, and F concatenates those subwords in their original left-to-right order. Their relative order is consequently preserved. This proves the observation.

Apply it to a=i and b=i+1. The event that i+1 precedes i in F(sigma) occurs exactly when both of the following hold:

(1) i+1 precedes i in sigma;
(2) at least one letter greater than i+1 lies between them in sigma.

Let k=n-i-1 be the number of letters greater than i+1. Delete all letters other than i, i+1, and these k greater letters. Their relative order is a uniform permutation of k+2 distinct letters. Condition (2) fails exactly when i and i+1 are adjacent in this reduced permutation. The probability of adjacency is

\[
\frac{2(k+1)!}{(k+2)!}=\frac{2}{k+2}.
\]

Swapping the labels i and i+1 preserves adjacency or nonadjacency and reverses which of them comes first. Therefore exactly half of the nonadjacent cases satisfy (1). It follows that

\[
\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{pos}_{F(\sigma)}(i+1)
 <\operatorname{pos}_{F(\sigma)}(i)\bigr)
=\frac12\left(1-\frac{2}{n-i+1}\right)
=\frac12-\frac{1}{n-i+1}.
\]

By linearity of expectation, with H_n denoting the nth harmonic number,

\[
X=\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}\left(\frac12-\frac{1}{n-i+1}\right)
=\frac{n-1}{2}-(H_n-1)
=\frac{n+1}{2}-H_n.
\]

For completeness, I give elementary rigorous bounds sufficient to take the floor at the specified large n, without relying on floating-point evaluation. I will show

\[
\frac{55}{2}<H_{10^{12}}<\frac{57}{2}.
\]

The identity

\[
\log\frac{1+t}{1-t}
=2\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}\frac{t^{2j+1}}{2j+1}
\qquad (0<t<1)
\]

follows by integrating the geometric series for 2/(1-t^2). All its terms are positive. Substituting t=1/2 gives the series for log 3, while t=1/19 gives the series for log(10/9). Thus

\[
\begin{aligned}
\log 10
&=2\log 3+\log(10/9)\\
&>2\left(1+\frac1{12}+\frac1{80}+\frac1{448}\right)+\frac2{19}\\
&=\frac{23}{10}+\frac{89}{63840}
>\frac{23}{10}.
\end{aligned}
\]

For an upper bound, the tail of the log 3 series starting at j=2 is strictly less than the geometric bound obtained by replacing all its denominators by 5. Hence

\[
\log 3
<1+\frac1{12}+\frac25\sum_{j=2}^{\infty}(1/2)^{2j+1}
=1+\frac1{12}+\frac1{60}
=\frac{11}{10}.
\]

Similarly, replacing all the denominators in the other series by 1 gives

\[
\log(10/9)
<2\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}(1/19)^{2j+1}
=\frac{19}{180}.
\]

Consequently

\[
\log 10<\frac{11}{5}+\frac{19}{180}=\frac{83}{36}.
\]

Since 1/x is decreasing, integral comparison gives

\[
H_n>\log n
\quad\text{and}\quad
H_n\leq H_{10}+\int_{10}^{n}\frac{dx}{x}
=H_{10}+\log(n/10)
\qquad(n\geq 10).
\]

At n=10^{12}, using H_10=7381/2520, these bounds imply

\[
H_n>12\cdot\frac{23}{10}=\frac{138}{5}>\frac{55}{2},
\]

and

\[
H_n<\frac{7381}{2520}+11\cdot\frac{83}{36}
=\frac{71291}{2520}
<\frac{71820}{2520}=\frac{57}{2}.
\]

Finally n/2=500000000000, so

\[
X=500000000000+\frac12-H_n.
\]

The bounds just proved give

\[
499999999972<X<499999999973.
\]

Therefore

\[
\boxed{\lfloor X\rfloor=499999999972}.
\]

CRITIC review

Verdict: I find no concrete mathematical error or missing closure step in the retained attempt. Its answer, \(\lfloor X\rfloor=499999999972\), follows from its exact expectation formula and its rigorous harmonic-number bounds. The following checks explain why; this verdict does not rely on the attempt's stated confidence.

1. The relative-order observation is valid.

For two letters \(a<b\), follow the recursive subword containing both letters. A maximum outside the interval between their positions removes only material on one side and leaves both endpoints in one recursive child. Thus the process eventually reaches a maximum in their interval. If that maximum is \(b\), the output puts \(b\) after every other letter of that subword, including \(a\). If the maximum is an interior letter larger than \(b\), the endpoints lie in different children. The output concatenates the left child's output before the right child's output, preserving the endpoints' original left-to-right order. Later concatenations cannot change their relative order. This accounts for outside letters and for either original ordering of the endpoints.

Consequently an inversion between \(i+1\) and \(i\) in the output occurs precisely when \(i+1\) was originally first and their original interval contained a letter larger than \(i+1\). There is no unaccounted case in this event characterization.

2. The probability calculation is valid.

The restriction of a uniform random permutation to any fixed collection of letters has uniform relative order. Restricting here to the two endpoints and the \(k=n-i-1\) larger letters turns the absence of a larger intervening letter into adjacency of the two endpoints. Contracting their adjacent pair, with its two possible orientations, gives \(2(k+1)!\) orders among \((k+2)!\) total orders. Swapping only the endpoint labels is a fixed-point-free pairing of the nonadjacent orders that reverses endpoint orientation and preserves nonadjacency. Hence the relevant probability is

\[
\frac12\left(1-\frac{2}{k+2}\right)
=\frac12-\frac{1}{n-i+1}.
\]

The edge case \(i=n-1\), where \(k=0\), gives zero as required because the maximum \(n\) is always last. No independence between different values of \(i\) is needed: linearity of expectation suffices. The sum of reciprocal terms runs over denominators \(n,n-1,\ldots,2\), so the exact expectation is indeed

\[
X=\frac{n-1}{2}-(H_n-1)=\frac{n+1}{2}-H_n.
\]

3. The numerical enclosure is rigorous and its arithmetic checks out.

The positive-term logarithm series used in the attempt follows from the geometric series by integration on a compact interval inside \((-1,1)\). At \(t=1/2\), its first four terms are \(1,1/12,1/80,1/448\). The lower-bound sum satisfies

\[
2\left(1+\frac1{12}+\frac1{80}+\frac1{448}\right)+\frac2{19}
=\frac{146921}{63840}
=\frac{23}{10}+\frac{89}{63840}.
\]

Omitted positive terms make the bound strict. For the upper bound on \(\log 3\), replacing denominators in the tail starting at \(j=2\) by 5 gives a tail of \(1/60\). Equality at its first term does not prevent strictness, since subsequent denominators are strictly larger than 5. Thus \(\log 3<11/10\). Likewise the geometric bound for \(\log(10/9)\) is strictly less than \(19/180\), because denominators after its first term exceed 1. Therefore

\[
\frac{23}{10}<\log 10<\frac{83}{36}.
\]

For decreasing \(1/x\), the integral on each interval \([j-1,j]\), \(j\ge 11\), is at least \(1/j\), which verifies the direction of the attempt's upper integral comparison. The lower comparison \(H_n>\log n\) is also valid. With \(H_{10}=7381/2520\) and \(n=10^{12}\), they yield

\[
H_n>12\cdot\frac{23}{10}=\frac{138}{5}>\frac{55}{2},
\]

and

\[
H_n<\frac{7381}{2520}+11\cdot\frac{83}{36}
=\frac{71291}{2520}<\frac{71820}{2520}=\frac{57}{2}.
\]

These bounds need not approximate \(H_n\) closely: they enclose it strictly between the two half-integers relevant to taking this floor. Subtracting them from \(500000000000+1/2\) reverses the inequalities and gives precisely

\[
499999999972<X<499999999973.
\]

Thus the requested floor is established. I have no substantive correction to propose.

SUPPORTED — NON-FORMAL independent mathematical review.

I reviewed the exact retained FINAL argument supplied in the sealed POSTREVIEW prompt. Its proof establishes floor(X) = 499999999972 for n = 1000000000000. The arithmetic-only checker's matching answer is not my basis for accepting the proof. I find no essential gap or incorrect mathematical step in the written argument.

1. Recursive interval lemma.

The recursive transformation preserves every letter exactly once, by induction on word length: the disjoint left and right subwords supply their letters, and their common maximum is appended once. Thus the output positions and relative orders in the question are well defined.

For fixed letters a < b, the proof correctly follows the contiguous recursive subword containing both endpoints until its maximum lies in the interval between their positions. While a maximum lies outside that interval, both endpoints and their entire intervening interval remain in the same child. That child is strictly shorter. Consequently this process must terminate, and the first maximum lying within the interval is the maximum of that interval. It cannot be a, since b is also in the interval.

If this maximum is b, the local output is F(L)F(R)b, so a precedes b, regardless of their original orientation. If the maximum is an interior letter, it is greater than b, the endpoints occupy different children, and F(L) is concatenated before F(R). Their relative order is therefore their original left-to-right order. Ancestor concatenations cannot change a relative order already established inside a child output. These cases prove both directions of the claimed equivalence:

  b precedes a in F(w)
  iff b precedes a in w and some letter greater than b lies between them.

In particular, smaller intervening letters do not affect this criterion. The interval reasoning does not rely on the arithmetic checker or on an unproved probabilistic property of F.

2. Uniform relative order and counting.

For a = i and b = i+1, there are exactly k = n-i-1 larger letters. Restricting a uniform permutation to these k+2 distinct letters gives a uniform relative order: each fixed restricted order has the same number of full-permutation extensions. No greater intervening letter occurs exactly when a and b are adjacent in this restriction. Contracting the pair gives k+1 objects; there are (k+1)! orders for each of the two pair orientations. Hence adjacency has probability 2(k+1)!/(k+2)! = 2/(k+2).

On the complementary, nonadjacent event, exchanging the two endpoint labels leaves nonadjacency unchanged and switches their orientation. This is a bijection without fixed points, so exactly half of the nonadjacent orders have b before a. Combining this with the proved interval lemma gives

  P(pos_F(sigma)(i+1) < pos_F(sigma)(i))
    = (1/2)(1-2/(k+2))
    = 1/2 - 1/(n-i+1).

The endpoint case k=0 is covered: all restricted orders are adjacent, and the probability is zero. There is no assumption that different descent events are independent.

3. Expectation.

The count in the question is the sum of its n-1 indicator variables. Linearity of expectation gives the displayed sum of probabilities. As i runs from 1 to n-1, n-i+1 runs from n down to 2, so the reciprocal sum is H_n-1. Therefore

  X = (n-1)/2 - (H_n-1) = (n+1)/2 - H_n.

All indices and the constant term are correct.

4. Logarithm enclosures.

For 0<t<1, the geometric series for 2/(1-u^2) is uniformly convergent on 0<=u<=t, which justifies termwise integration. Its integral is log((1+t)/(1-t)), yielding the stated positive-term series. The substitutions t=1/2 and t=1/19 give log 3 and log(10/9), respectively, and log 10 = 2 log 3 + log(10/9) is correct.

The lower bound retains four terms for log 3 and one for log(10/9). Each omitted tail is positive, so the inequalities are strict. The explicit arithmetic is

  1 + 1/12 + 1/80 + 1/448 = 7379/6720,
  2(7379/6720) + 2/19 = 146921/63840,
  146921/63840 = 23/10 + 89/63840 > 23/10.

For the upper bound on log 3, replacing denominators 2j+1 by 5 for j>=2 is an upper bound, with strictness supplied by every j>2 term. The geometric tail is

  sum_{j=2}^infinity (1/2)^(2j+1) = (1/32)/(1-1/4) = 1/24.

It follows that log 3 < 1+1/12+(2/5)(1/24) = 11/10. Replacing every series denominator for log(10/9) by 1 is likewise strictly larger, because the j>=1 terms have larger actual denominators. Thus

  log(10/9) < (2/19)/(1-1/361) = 19/180,
  log 10 < 11/5 + 19/180 = 83/36.

The retained FINAL's particular rational bounds are valid independently of the different rational enclosure displayed in the arithmetic-checker evidence.

5. Harmonic enclosure and the floor.

The integral comparisons have the correct directions. On [j,j+1], 1/x < 1/j away from the left endpoint, so log n < H_{n-1} < H_n for this n>1. On [j-1,j], 1/x > 1/j away from the right endpoint, so each reciprocal term for j>=11 is bounded above by that interval's integral. Summing gives H_n <= H_10 + log(n/10), as written; the non-strict version suffices.

Direct summation for H_10 gives numerator

  2520+1260+840+630+504+420+360+315+280+252 = 7381

over denominator 2520. With n=10^12, log n = 12 log 10 and log(n/10) = 11 log 10. The resulting bounds are

  H_n > 12(23/10) = 138/5 > 55/2,
  H_n < 7381/2520 + 11(83/36)
      = (7381+63910)/2520 = 71291/2520
      < 71820/2520 = 57/2.

Strictness in the upper enclosure follows from the strict logarithm bound even if the preceding integral comparison is written non-strictly. Finally (n+1)/2 = 500000000000+1/2. Subtracting 55/2 < H_n < 57/2 reverses the relevant inequality directions and gives

  499999999972 < X < 499999999973.

This proves the claimed floor without requiring a closer numerical estimate of H_n.

task.title: A recursive construction on large permutations
task.statement: Let W be the finite words of distinct positive integers. Define F(empty)=empty. If w=L m R with maximum letter m, define F(w)=F(L)F(R)m. Let sigma be uniformly random among permutations of {1,...,n}, n=1000000000000. Let X=E[#{i:1<=i<n, pos_F(sigma)(i+1)<pos_F(sigma)(i)}]. Compute floor(X), with a complete mathematical justification.
